Step 5: Decrease in time = $T - \frac{10}{11}T = \frac{1}{11}T$. Percentage decrease = $\frac{1}{11} \times 100 \approx 9.09\% \approx 9\%$.

questions.q: A parachutist after bailing out falls for 10s without friction. When the parachute opens he descends with an acceleration of $2\text{ m/s}^{2}$ against his direction and reached the ground with $4\text{ m/s}$. From what height he has dropped himself? $(g=10\text{m/s}^{2})$
questions.sol:
Step 1: Phase 1 (Free Fall): Starts from rest ($u=0$), $t=10\text{s}$, $a=10\text{ m/s}^2$.
Step 2: Distance fallen: $h_1 = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10)(10^2) = 500\text{ m}$.
Step 3: Velocity at parachute deployment: $v_1 = u + gt = 0 + 10(10) = 100\text{ m/s}$.
Step 4: Phase 2 (Parachute): Initial velocity $u_2 = 100\text{ m/s}$, final velocity $v_2 = 4\text{ m/s}$, acceleration $a = -2\text{ m/s}^2$.
Step 5: Remaining distance $h_2$: $v_2^2 - u_2^2 = 2ah_2 \implies 4^2 - 100^2 = 2(-2)h_2$.
Step 6: $16 - 10000 = -4h_2 \implies -9984 = -4h_2 \implies h_2 = 2496\text{ m}$.
Step 7: Total height dropped $= h_1 + h_2 = 500 + 2496 = 2996\text{ m}$.

questions.q: A body is dropped from the roof of a multi-storied building. It passes the ceiling of the 15th storey at a speed of $20\text{ ms}^{-1}$. If the height of each storey is 4m, the number of storeys in the building is (take $g=10\text{ms}^{-2}$ and neglect air resistance):
questions.sol:
Step 1: Calculate the total distance fallen from the roof to reach a velocity of $20\text{ m/s}$.
Step 2: Use $v^2 - u^2 = 2gS$. Since it's dropped, $u=0$.
Step 3: $20^2 = 2(10)S \implies 400 = 20S \implies S = 20\text{ m}$.
Step 4: Convert the distance to storeys: $20\text{ m} / 4\text{ m/storey} = 5\text{ storeys}$. The body has fallen 5 storeys.
Step 5: Passing the *ceiling* of the 15th storey means there are exactly 15 storeys still below the ball (storeys 15 down to 1).
Step 6: Total storeys in building = Storeys fallen + Storeys below = $5 + 15 = 20$.

questions.q: A body is projected vertically up with velocity $98\text{ms}^{-1}$. After 2 s if the acceleration due to gravity of earth disappears, the velocity of the body at the end of next 3 s is:
questions.sol:
Step 1: Calculate the velocity of the body exactly 2 seconds after projection.
Step 2: Use $v = u - gt$. Since $u = 98\text{ m/s}$, we get $v = 98 - (9.8)(2) = 98 - 19.6 = 78.4\text{ m/s}$.
Step 3: At this exact instant, the problem states that gravity disappears, making the net acceleration $a = 0$.
Step 4: By Newton's First Law, an object in motion will maintain its velocity unless acted upon by an external force.
Step 5: Since $a=0$, the velocity remains constant for the next 3 seconds.
Step 6: Therefore, the velocity is $78.4\text{ ms}^{-1}$.

questions.q: An elevator is going up. The variation in the velocity of the elevator is as given in the graph. What is the height to which the elevator takes the passengers?
questions.sol:
Step 1: The height (displacement) is given by the area under the velocity-time graph.
Step 2: The graph forms a trapezium with the parallel sides on the time axis.
Step 3: The bottom base is the total time interval: $b_1 = 12\text{ s} - 0\text{ s} = 12\text{ s}$.
Step 4: The top base is the interval of constant velocity: $b_2 = 10\text{ s} - 2\text{ s} = 8\text{ s}$.
Step 5: The height of the trapezium is the maximum velocity: $h = 3.6\text{ m/s}$.
Step 6: Area $= \frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2) \times h = \frac{1}{2}(12 + 8) \times 3.6 = \frac{1}{2}(20) \times 3.6 = 10 \times 3.6 = 36.0\text{ m}$.

questions.q: The velocity time graph of a body moving in a straight line is shown in the figure. The displacement and distance travelled by the body in 6 sec are respectively (in metres).
questions.sol:
Step 1: Calculate the area of each rectangular block on the graph.
Step 2: Area 1 (0 to 2s): $A_1 = 4 \times 2 = 8\text{ m}$.
Step 3: Area 2 (2 to 4s): $A_2 = -2 \times 2 = -4\text{ m}$.
Step 4: Area 3 (4 to 6s): $A_3 = 2 \times 2 = 4\text{ m}$.
Step 5: Displacement is the algebraic sum of the areas: $8 + (-4) + 4 = 8\text{ m}$.
Step 6: Distance is the sum of the absolute magnitudes of the areas: $|8| + |-4| + |4| = 8 + 4 + 4 = 16\text{ m}$.

questions.q: The velocity-time graph of a stone thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of $30\text{ ms}^{-1}$ is shown in the figure. The velocity in the upward direction is taken as positive and that in the downward direction as negative. What is the maximum height to which the stone rises?
questions.sol:
Step 1: The maximum height is achieved when the velocity of the stone becomes exactly zero (at $t=3\text{s}$ according to the graph).
Step 2: The height is represented by the area under the velocity-time graph from $t=0$ to $t=3$.
Step 3: The graph forms a right-angled triangle with a base of 3s and a height of $30\text{ m/s}$.
Step 4: Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.
Step 5: Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 30 = 45\text{ m}$.

questions.q: The variation of velocity of particle moving along a straight line is shown in the figure. The distance travelled by the particle in 4s is
questions.sol:
Step 1: Find the area under the curve for each 1-second interval shown in the graph.
Step 2: 0 to 1s (Triangle): Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 20 = 10\text{ m}$.
Step 3: 1 to 2s (Rectangle): Area $= 1 \times 20 = 20\text{ m}$.
Step 4: 2 to 3s (Trapezium): Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times (20 + 10) \times 1 = 15\text{ m}$.
Step 5: 3 to 4s (Rectangle): Area $= 1 \times 10 = 10\text{ m}$.
Step 6: Total distance $= 10 + 20 + 15 + 10 = 55\text{ m}$.

questions.q: Velocity-time (v-t) graph for a moving object is shown in the figure. Total displacement of the object during the time interval when there is non-zero acceleration and retardation is
questions.sol:
Step 1: Identify the intervals with non-zero acceleration/retardation from the graph. These are the segments where the velocity is changing: 20s to 30s and 30s to 40s.
Step 2: Calculate the area of the trapezium for the acceleration phase (20 to 30s). Base $= 10\text{s}$, parallel sides are $1$ and $4$. Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (1 + 4) = 5 \times 5 = 25\text{ m}$.
Step 3: Calculate the area of the trapezium for the retardation phase (30 to 40s). Base $= 10\text{s}$, parallel sides are $4$ and $1$. Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (4 + 1) = 5 \times 5 = 25\text{ m}$.
Step 4: Total displacement during these specific intervals $= 25 + 25 = 50\text{ m}$.

questions.q: An armored car 2m long and 3 m wide is moving at $10\text{ ms}^{-1}$ along its length when a bullet hits it in a direction making an angle $\tan^{-1}(3/4)$ with the length of the car as seen by a stationary observer. The bullet enters one edge of the car at the corner and passes out at the diagonally opposite corner. Neglecting gravity, the time for the bullet to cross the car is:
questions.sol:
Step 1: Let the car move along the x-axis: $\vec{v}_c = 10\hat{i}$.
Step 2: Bullet velocity relative to ground is $\vec{v}_b = v_b \cos\theta\hat{i} + v_b \sin\theta\hat{j}$. Since $\tan\theta = 3/4$, we have $\cos\theta = 4/5$ and $\sin\theta = 3/5$. So, $\vec{v}_b = \frac{4v_b}{5}\hat{i} + \frac{3v_b}{5}\hat{j}$.
Step 3: Bullet velocity relative to the car is $\vec{v}_{bc} = \vec{v}_b - \vec{v}_c = \left(\frac{4v_b}{5} - 10\right)\hat{i} + \left(\frac{3v_b}{5}\right)\hat{j}$.
Step 4: To pass diagonally from $(0,0)$ to $(2,3)$ relative to the car, the relative velocity vector must be parallel to the diagonal $2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$. Thus, $\frac{v_{y}}{v_{x}} = \frac{3}{2}$.
Step 5: Set up the proportion: $\frac{3v_b/5}{4v_b/5 - 10} = \frac{3}{2} \implies 2\left(\frac{3v_b}{5}\right) = 3\left(\frac{4v_b}{5} - 10\right) \implies \frac{6v_b}{5} = \frac{12v_b}{5} - 30$.
Step 6: Solve for $v_b$: $\frac{6v_b}{5} = 30 \implies v_b = 25\text{ m/s}$.
Step 7: Substitute back to find relative x-velocity: $v_{x} = \frac{4(25)}{5} - 10 = 20 - 10 = 10\text{ m/s}$.
Step 8: Time to cross the 2m length is $t = \frac{2}{10} = 0.20\text{ s}$.

questions.q: Two particles start simultaneously from the same point and move along two straight lines. One with uniform velocity v and other with a uniform acceleration a. If $\alpha$ is the angle between the lines of motion of two particles then the least value of relative velocity will be at time given by:
questions.sol:
Step 1: Let particle 1 move along the x-axis: $\vec{v}_1 = v\hat{i}$.
Step 2: Particle 2 starts from rest and accelerates at angle $\alpha$: $\vec{v}_2 = (at\cos\alpha)\hat{i} + (at\sin\alpha)\hat{j}$.
Step 3: The relative velocity vector is $\vec{v}_{rel} = \vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2 = (v - at\cos\alpha)\hat{i} - (at\sin\alpha)\hat{j}$.
Step 4: The square of the magnitude is $V^2 = (v - at\cos\alpha)^2 + (-at\sin\alpha)^2 = v^2 - 2vat\cos\alpha + a^2t^2\cos^2\alpha + a^2t^2\sin^2\alpha$.
Step 5: Simplify using $\sin^2\alpha + \cos^2\alpha = 1$: $V^2 = v^2 - 2vat\cos\alpha + a^2t^2$.
Step 6: To find the minimum relative velocity, differentiate $V^2$ with respect to time $t$ and set it to zero: $\frac{d(V^2)}{dt} = -2va\cos\alpha + 2a^2t = 0$.
Step 7: Solve for $t$: $2a^2t = 2va\cos\alpha \implies t = \frac{v\cos\alpha}{a}$.

questions.q: A jet airplane travelling at the speed of $500\text{ km/h}$ ejects its products of combustion at the speed of $1500\text{ km/h}$ relative to the jet plane. What is the velocity of the later (exhaust gas) with respect to an observer on the ground?
questions.sol:
Step 1: Establish a sign convention. Let the direction of the jet airplane be positive. Velocity of the jet relative to ground $\vec{v}_j = +500\text{ km/h}$.
Step 2: The exhaust gas is ejected backwards. So, the velocity of the exhaust gas relative to the jet is $\vec{v}_{ej} = -1500\text{ km/h}$.
Step 3: We need the velocity of the exhaust gas relative to the ground ($\vec{v}_e$). Use the relative velocity formula: $\vec{v}_{ej} = \vec{v}_e - \vec{v}_j$.
Step 4: Rearrange to solve for $\vec{v}_e$: $\vec{v}_e = \vec{v}_{ej} + \vec{v}_j$.
Step 5: Substitute the values: $\vec{v}_e = -1500 + 500 = -1000\text{ km/h}$.
